newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Brussels bourse acts on insider trading.
newsitem.headline: Brussels bourse acts on insider trading.

text.p: The Brussels bourse said on Friday that in its first year of acting as front-line market regulator it decided to send four cases of suspected insider trading to the judicial authorities and was considering others.
Under a wide reform to make the bourse more competitive and modern, a management committee early last year replaced the Belgian Banking and Finance Commission as the first market regulator.
The exchange said on Friday that in the course of its surveillance activities in 1996, begun in March, it had started analysing 88 cases, of which 23 lead to further enquiries.
By the end of 1996 offences or indications of offences had been found in eight of the 23 cases.

The bourse had found possible insider trading in four cases which it had passed on to the public prosecutor, and was still considering seven more. Other suspicions included suspected fraud and share price manipulation.
It did not name any companies involved.
In its enquiries the bourse had requested information from market authorities in Luxembourg, Britain, Germany and the Netherlands, as well as questioning various intermediaries.
The report referred to two cases of price sensitive information being given to analysts before wider publication.
It also highlighted the problem of sensitive information being known by individuals in a company before it was published.
The bourse recommended company boards draw up internal rules to prevent anyone who might have inside information from buying or selling the company's shares during a pre-set period.

Separately, the bourse is looking at ways to limit volatility in the Bel-20 leading share index, in response to sporadic wild swings during the last minutes of trading. It has already announced plans to introduce a circuit breaker, possibly before the second half of the year.
Olivier Lefebvre, head of the bourse's management committee, told a news conference to present the report that 1996 had been a good year generally for the exchange.
After the recent structural modernisation, Lefebvre said improving liquidation was now a priority.
This would include amongst other things extending the guarantee of completion of orders, whereby the risk of counterparties was taken by a third party, to the cash market.
Also, the launch of a system of registered bonds would facilitate the liquidation of transactions on a pre-established date.

"The reform of the liquidation system must (also) take account of international recomendations so as to facilitate exchanges with international clearing and settlement organisations (such as Euroclear, Cedel), something which would be an attraction for foreign parties," the report said.
Lefebvre noted that in 1996 Brussels had seen record market volume of 808.8 billion francs, up 48 percent from 1995.
Market capitalisation for the main market rose by 27.5 percent to reach 3,806 billion fancs at the end of 1996, or 46 percent of Belgian gross domestic product.
This was largely because of a general increase in share prices, the issuing of new shares, and several bourse listings.
Lefebvre said that in 1997 about 10 Belgian companies could be expected to come to the market.

In 1996 four Belgian companies were brought to the main market, including Dexia-Credit Communal which with a bourse capitalisation of 106 billion Belgian francs was the largest. Two more were promoted from the second market.
